Topic 2 — The Buck Converter

Analysis and design of a buck–boost converter

Erickson, Problem 2.1  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsThe whole Topic 2 method on a converter you have not seen: volt-second balance for V, charge balance for I, then size L and C to a ripple spec.
Assigned: Parts (a)–(c).
Parts (d) and (e) sketch the transistor and diode currents, which needs the switch realization from Topic 3 — come back to them after that.

Analysis and design of a buck–boost converter: A buck–boost converter is illustrated in Fig. 2.28a, and a practical implementation using a transistor and diode is shown in Fig. 2.28b.

(a)Find the dependence of the equilibrium output voltage V and inductor current I on the duty ratio D, input voltage Vg, and load resistance R. You may assume that the inductor current ripple and capacitor voltage ripple are small.
(b)Plot your results of part (a) over the range 0 ≤ D ≤ 1.
(c)Dc design: for the specifications
Vg = 30 VV = −20 V
R = 4 Ωfs = 40 kHz
(i)Find D and I
(ii)Calculate the value of L that will make the peak-to-peak inductor current ripple Δi equal to ten percent of the average inductor current I.
(iii)Choose C such that the peak-to-peak output voltage ripple Δv is 0.1 V.
(d)Sketch the transistor drain current waveform iT(t) for your design of part (c). Include the effects of inductor current ripple. What is the peak value of iT? Also sketch iT(t) for the case when L is decreased such that Δi is 50% of I. What happens to the peak value of iT in this case?
(e)Sketch the diode current waveform iD(t) for the two cases of part (d).
Final answer
(a)V = −D·Vg/(1 − D), I = D·Vg/((1 − D)²·R)
(b)V/Vg = −D/(1 − D): 0 at D = 0, −1 at D = 0.5, → −∞ as D → 1.
(c)(i) D = 0.4, I = 8.33 A; (ii) L = 360 µH; (iii) C = 500 µF
(d)Peak iT = 8.75 A with Δi = 10 % of I; 10.4 A with Δi = 50 % of I.
(e)Peak iD equals the peak iT in each case.
Topic 2 — The Buck Converter

H-bridge converter — conversion ratio

Erickson, Problem 2.5  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsVolt-second balance alone, on an unfamiliar converter and with no numbers to hide behind. The H-bridge also turns up again in Topic 7 (Single-Phase Inverters).

The switches in the converter of Fig. 2.31 operate synchronously: each is in position 1 for 0 < t < DTs, and in position 2 for DTs < t < Ts. Derive an expression for the voltage conversion ratio M(D) = V/Vg. Sketch M(D) vs. D.

Final answer

M(D) = 2D − 1

Topic 2 — The Buck Converter

H-bridge converter — the ripples

Erickson, Problem 2.7  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsThe small-ripple approximation used the other way round: from the switching waveforms to ΔiL and ΔvC.
Same converter as 2.5 — do them together.

For the converter of Fig. 2.31, derive expressions for the inductor current ripple ΔiL and the capacitor voltage ripple ΔvC.

Final answer

ΔiL = 2D(1 − D)·Vg·Ts/L and ΔvC = D(1 − D)·Vg·Ts²/(4LC), both peak-to-peak.

Topic 2 — The Buck Converter

Current-fed bridge converter — dc inductor current

Erickson, Problem 2.8  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsCapacitor charge balance on its own. This is the one problem that isolates the tool you used to get I = V/R for the buck.

For the converter of Fig. 2.32, derive an analytical expression for the dc component of the inductor current, I, as a function of D, Vg, and R. Sketch your result vs. D.

Final answer

I = Vg/(R·(2D − 1)²)

Topic 2 — The Buck Converter

Conversion ratio of a two-inductor converter

F2025 Midterm, Problem 6  ·  ENEL 585 Fall 2025 midterm (6 November 2025, 1 h 50 min, 48 marks)
What it drillsVolt-second balance on two inductors at once, under exam conditions: the same method as 2.1 and 2.5, on a converter with a capacitor in the power path.
Last year's midterm question: 6 of 48 marks, so about 14 minutes. Try it timed.

The converter shown below operates in continuous conduction mode (CCM). All components are ideal, and the capacitors are large enough that their voltage ripple is small. The load is represented by R.

Switching intervals:

  • 0 → DTs: switch S is on and diode D is off
  • DTs → Ts: switch S is off and diode D is on
(a)Derive the steady-state voltage conversion ratio M(D) = V/Vg. [4 marks]
(b)Describe how the output voltage varies with respect to the input as the duty ratio is varied. [2 marks]
Final answer
(a)M(D) = V/Vg = −D/(1 − D)
(b)The output is inverted: |V| < Vg for D < 0.5, |V| = Vg at D = 0.5, |V| > Vg for D > 0.5.
Topic 3 — Choosing L, the Boost Converter, Output Ripple, DCM

Boost converter operating point and the MOSFET voltage

Erickson, Problem 2.2  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsThe boost conversion ratio at a real operating point, then reading the switch voltage waveform off the two states.

The boost converter illustrated in Fig. 2.29 operates with the following conditions:

Input voltageVg = 3.3 V
Output voltageV = 5 V
Switching frequencyfs = 500 kHz

All elements are ideal, and the converter operates in steady state with waveforms similar to those illustrated in Fig. 2.15.

(a)What is the duty cycle?
(b)Sketch the waveform of the MOSFET drain-to-source voltage. Label the numerical values of all relevant times and voltages.
(c)Find the dc component of the voltage waveform of Part (b).
Fig. 2.15 is the boost inductor voltage and current waveform — the pair you drew in class on “Inductor Volt-Second Balance: Solving for V”.
Final answer
(a)D = 0.34
(b)vDS = 0 V for 0.68 µs, then 5 V for 1.32 µs (Ts = 2 µs).
(c)3.3 V
Topic 3 — Choosing L, the Boost Converter, Output Ripple, DCM

Buck converter with a synchronous rectifier at light load

Erickson, Problem 5.3  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsWhy DCM happens at all. The diode's one-way conduction is what creates the third state — take the diode away and the argument changes.
Five minutes, and it links the synchronous buck straight to the DCM discussion.

A certain buck converter contains a synchronous rectifier, as described in Sect. 4.1.5.

(a)Does this converter operate in the discontinuous conduction mode at light load? Explain.
(b)The load resistance is disconnected (R → ∞), and the converter is operated with duty cycle 0.5. Sketch the inductor current waveform.
Final answer
(a)No: it stays in CCM at any load.
(b)V = Vg/2; iL is a triangle centred on 0 A, from −Vg·Ts/(8L) to +Vg·Ts/(8L).
Topic 3 — Choosing L, the Boost Converter, Output Ripple, DCM

DCM buck–boost converter

Erickson, Problem 5.1  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsThe full DCM run — mode boundary, then M(D,K) — on the buck–boost, exactly parallel to the buck you did in class.

The elements of the buck–boost converter of Fig. 5.21 are ideal: all losses may be ignored. Your results for parts (a) and (b) should agree with Table 5.2.

(a)Show that the converter operates in discontinuous conduction mode when K < Kcrit, and derive expressions for K and Kcrit.
(b)Derive an expression for the dc conversion ratio V/Vg of the buck–boost converter operating in discontinuous conduction mode.
(c)For K = 0.1, plot V/Vg over the entire range 0 ≤ D ≤ 1.
(d)Sketch the inductor voltage and current waveforms for K = 0.1 and D = 0.3. Label salient features.
(e)What happens to V at no load (R → ∞)? Explain why, physically.
Final answer
(a)K = 2L/(R·Ts), Kcrit = (1 − D)²; DCM when K < Kcrit.
(b)V/Vg = −D/√K
(c)DCM for D < 0.684, where M = −3.16·D; CCM above, where M = −D/(1 − D). Both give −2.16 at the boundary.
(d)M = −0.949, D2 = 0.316, D3 = 0.384
(e)For any fixed D > 0 (e.g. D = 0.3 from (d)), |V| increases without limit (ideal components): each cycle transfers a fixed energy to C with no load to absorb it. Only D → 0, as a regulating loop would do, keeps V bounded.
Topic 3 — Choosing L, the Boost Converter, Output Ripple, DCM

Boost converter — the critical duty ratio

F2025 Midterm, Problem 7  ·  ENEL 585 Fall 2025 midterm (6 November 2025, 1 h 50 min, 48 marks)
What it drillsThe CCM/DCM boundary derived from scratch for the boost, then turned round into a condition on the duty ratio.
Last year's midterm question: 6 of 48 marks, so about 14 minutes. Try it timed.

Consider the boost converter shown below. All components are ideal.

Derive an expression for the critical duty ratio Dc (the boundary between CCM and DCM) in terms of Vg, V, L, R and Ts. State clearly which side of Dc is DCM. [6 marks]

Final answer

Dc = 2L·V²/(Vg²·R·Ts); DCM for D > Dc.

Topic 3 — Choosing L, the Boost Converter, Output Ripple, DCM

Buck converter mode boundary on the Vg–Pload plane

Erickson, Problem 5.19  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsThe CCM/DCM boundary as a design constraint rather than a formula: which operating points are on which side of it.
Do not also do 5.4 — it is the same converter and the same numbers, without the sketch. The book is inconsistent about the top of the input range: the problem says Vg ≤ 70 V, while the Vg axis of Fig. 5.30 is labelled 75 V. Work to 70 V.

An unregulated dc input voltage Vg varies over the range 35 V ≤ Vg ≤ 70 V. A buck converter reduces this voltage to 28 V; a feedback loop varies the duty cycle as necessary such that the converter output voltage is always equal to 28 V. The load power varies over the range 10 W ≤ Pload ≤ 1000 W. The buck converter elements are L = 22 µH, C = 470 µF, fs = 75 kHz. Losses may be ignored.

(a)Over what range of Vg and Pload does the converter operate in continuous conduction mode? Sketch the mode boundary on the axes of Fig. 5.30, and identify the region over which the converter operates in CCM.
(b)Determine the maximum and minimum values of the steady-state transistor duty cycle.
Final answer
(a)CCM for Pload > 237.6·(1 − 28/Vg) W: 47.5 W at Vg = 35 V, 142.5 W at Vg = 70 V. DCM below this curve.
(b)Dmax = 0.80 (Vg = 35 V, CCM); Dmin = 0.106 (Vg = 70 V, Pload = 10 W, DCM).
Topic 3 — Choosing L, the Boost Converter, Output Ripple, DCM

Design of a DCM boost converter

Erickson, Problem 5.17  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsBoost, DCM and component sizing in one: hold K below Kcrit across the whole operating range, then size C to a ripple spec.

A DCM boost converter as in Fig. 5.12 is to be designed to operate under the following conditions:

18 V ≤ Vg ≤ 36 V
5 W ≤ Pload ≤ 100 W
V = 48 V
fs = 150 kHz

You may assume that a feedback loop will vary to transistor duty cycle as necessary to maintain a constant output voltage of 48 V.

Design the converter, subject to the following considerations:

  • The converter should operate in the discontinuous conduction mode at all times. To ensure an adequate design margin, the inductance L should be chosen such that K is no greater than 75% of Kcrit at all operating points.
  • Given the above requirements, choose the element values to minimize the peak inductor current.
  • The peak-to-peak output voltage ripple should be less than 1 V.

Specify:

(a)The inductor value L
(b)The output capacitor value C
(c)The worst-case peak inductor current ipk
(d)The maximum and minimum values of the transistor duty cycle D.
(e)The values of D, K, and Kcrit at the following operating points: (i) Vg = 18 V and Pload = 5 W; (ii) Vg = 36 V and Pload = 5 W; (iii) Vg = 18 V and Pload = 100 W; (iv) Vg = 36 V and Pload = 100 W.
Fig. 5.12 is the boost converter drawn with a transistor and diode — the same circuit as Topic 3, “Another Two-Switch DC-DC Converter: the Boost Converter”.
Final answer

Ideal components assumed.

(a)L = 5.86 µH: the largest L that keeps K ≤ 0.75·Kcrit at every operating point (binding at Vg = 18 V, Pload = 100 W), which minimizes the peak current.
(b)C ≥ 9.5 µF
(c)ipk = 11.9 A
(d)Dmax = 0.582 (18 V, 100 W); Dmin = 0.041 (36 V, 5 W)
(e)(i) D = 0.130, K = 0.0038, Kcrit = 0.098
(ii)D = 0.041, K = 0.0038, Kcrit = 0.038
(iii)D = 0.582, K = 0.076, Kcrit = 0.102
(iv)D = 0.184, K = 0.076, Kcrit = 0.123
Topic 4 — Transformers

Tapped-inductor boost converter

Erickson, Problem 6.1  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsBuilding the magnetizing-inductance-plus-ideal-transformer model yourself, then running Topic 3's boost analysis on it.

Tapped-inductor boost converter. The boost converter is sometimes modified as illustrated in Fig. 6.43, to obtain a larger conversion ratio than would otherwise occur. The inductor winding contains a total of (n1 + n2) turns. The transistor is connected to a tap placed n1 turns from the left side of the inductor, as shown. The tapped inductor can be viewed as a two-winding (n1 : n2) transformer, in which the two windings are connected in series. The inductance of the entire (n1 + n2) turn winding is L.

(a)Sketch an equivalent circuit model for the tapped inductor, which includes a magnetizing inductance and an ideal transformer. Label the values of the magnetizing inductance and turns ratio.
(b)Determine an analytical expression for the conversion ratio M = V/Vg. You may assume that the transistor, diode, tapped inductor, and capacitor are lossless. You may also assume that the converter operates in continuous conduction mode.
(c)Sketch M(D) vs. D for n1 = n2, and compare to the nontapped (n2 = 0) case.
Final answer
(a)An ideal n1 : n2 transformer with magnetizing inductance L·n1²/(n1 + n2)² on the n1 winding (equivalently L across the whole winding).
(b)M = (1 + (n2/n1)·D)/(1 − D)
(c)n1 = n2: M = (1 + D)/(1 − D), e.g. 3 at D = 0.5, against 2 for the untapped boost.
Topic 5 — The Flyback Converter

Analysis of the DCM flyback converter

Erickson, Problem 6.2  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020)
What it drillsExactly what the last slide of Topic 5 leaves you to do: three subintervals, the mode boundary, then V and D₂.

Analysis of the DCM flyback converter. The flyback converter of Fig. 6.32d operates in the discontinuous conduction mode.

(a)Model the flyback transformer as a magnetizing inductance in parallel with an ideal transformer, and sketch the converter circuits during the three subintervals.
(b)Derive the conditions for operation in discontinuous conduction mode.
(c)Solve the converter: derive expressions for the steady-state output voltage V and subinterval 2 (diode conduction interval) duty cycle D2.
Fig. 6.32(d) is the flyback converter — the same circuit as Topic 5, “The Flyback Model We Analyse”.
Final answer

With K = 2Lm/(R·Ts) and Erickson's 1 : n transformer (n = N2/N1 in the Topic 5 N1 : N2 model, so both forms below are the same result):

(b)DCM when K < (1 − D)²/n² = (N1/N2)²·(1 − D)²
(c)V = D·Vg/√K (independent of the turns ratio); D2 = n·√K = (N2/N1)·√K
Topic 6 — AC Fundamentals

One frequency at a time

Practice, Problem A.1  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsThe Topic 6 rule that carries the rest of the course: solve each harmonic with its own impedance, then combine rms values and powers, never phasors at different frequencies.

A series load R = 8 Ω, L = 10 mH is connected to the voltage

v(t) = 100·cos(ω1t) + 20·cos(3ω1t + 30°) Vf1 = 60 Hz
(a)Find i(t).
(b)Find the rms value of i, the THD of i and the THD of v. Why is the current less distorted than the voltage?
(c)Find the average power delivered to the load, and the power factor kp seen by the source.
(d)Find cos θ1, where θ1 is the angle by which the fundamental of i lags the fundamental of v, and compare it with kp. Why are they not equal? Under what condition would they be equal?
Final answer
(a)i(t) = 11.31·cos(ω1t − 25.2°) + 1.44·cos(3ω1t − 24.7°) A
(b)Irms = 8.06 A; THD of i = 12.8 %; THD of v = 20 %. The inductor's impedance is three times larger at the third harmonic.
(c)P = 520 W; kp = 0.894
(d)cos θ1 = 0.905, slightly above kp = 0.894: the third harmonic adds more to Vrms·Irms than it adds to P. They are equal only when v and i are both pure sinusoids.
Topic 6 — AC Fundamentals

A converter connected to the grid

Practice, Problem A.2  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsThe source-into-grid example of Topic 6 run in both directions: from the power you want to the voltage you must produce, and back.
Phasors use peak magnitudes, as in the lectures, so the complex power is S = ½·V·I*.

A converter that produces the voltage phasor Vt is connected through an inductor to the grid. The current Ig is defined flowing from the converter, through the inductor, into the grid.

Vg = 340∠0° V (peak)ω1L = 2 Ω
(a)The grid is to absorb P = 4 kW and Q = +1 kvar. Find Ig and the Vt required.
(b)The converter instead produces Vt = 360∠8° V. Find Ig, and the real and reactive power absorbed by the grid.
(c)For the operating point of part (b), find the real and reactive power leaving the converter terminals. Account for the difference from part (b).
(d)Which of the magnitude and the angle of Vt mainly sets P, and which mainly sets Q? To help you answer, compare how much P and Q each change between parts (a) and (b), and how much the magnitude and the angle of Vt change.
Final answer
(a)Ig = 24.3∠−14.0° A; Vt = 354.9∠7.6° V (peak)
(b)Ig = 26.4∠−18.2° A; P = 4.26 kW, Q = +1.40 kvar
(c)P = 4.26 kW, Q = 2.10 kvar. The extra 0.70 kvar is absorbed by the inductor (½·ω1L·Îg²).
(d)The angle mainly sets P; the magnitude mainly sets Q.
Topic 6 — AC Fundamentals

Distorted current from a sinusoidal source

Practice, Problem A.3  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsPower factor as displacement factor times distortion factor.

A load connected to vs(t) = 170·sin(ω1t) V draws a square-wave current of amplitude 3 A whose zero crossings coincide with those of vs.

(a)Find the rms value of the fundamental of the current, its THD, and the average power. The THD includes all the harmonics: find it from the rms value of the whole current and the rms value of its fundamental, rather than by summing harmonics.
(b)Find the displacement factor, the distortion factor and the power factor.
(c)The current is now delayed by 30° with its shape unchanged. Find the new power and power factor.
Final answer
(a)I1 = 2.70 A rms; THD = 48.3 %; P = 325 W
(b)Displacement factor 1; distortion factor 0.900; kp = 0.900
(c)P = 281 W; kp = 0.780
Topic 7 — Single-Phase Inverters

A square-wave inverter with an output filter

Kassakian, Problem 2.14  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsSquare-wave harmonics, then one frequency at a time through a second-order filter.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Note the 50 Hz output.

The bridge shown connects a battery vd to a resistive load that needs a sinusoidal voltage at 50 Hz. The switches are operated so that the bridge output vt is a square wave of amplitude vd at 50 Hz. An inductor L in series and a capacitor C across the load filter it.

vd = 100 VL = 12 mH
C = 32 µFR = 10 Ω

Find the amplitudes of the fundamental and third-harmonic components of the load voltage vac.

Final answer

Square-wave amplitudes 4vd/(kπ): 127.3 V and 42.4 V.

The filter gain is 0.968 at 50 Hz and 0.764 at 150 Hz, so the load voltage has a fundamental of 123 V and a third harmonic of 32.4 V (peak).

Topic 7 — Single-Phase Inverters

Removing a harmonic with phase-shift control

Kassakian, Problem 8.4  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsThe cos(kπα) factor of phase-shift control, used to place a zero on a chosen harmonic and to see what that costs the others.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Kassakian measures the zero state as an angle δ on each side of a zero crossing, so each zero interval is 2δ wide and δ = πα; the book's answer is δ = 12.9°.

A full bridge supplied from vd feeds a resistive load with phase-shift control. Its output vt is the three-level waveform shown: +vd, 0 and −vd, with vt equal to zero for an interval αT1 centred on every zero crossing.

Find the value of α that eliminates the seventh harmonic of the load voltage. For that α, calculate the amplitudes of the third and fifth harmonics, and compare them with the corresponding amplitudes of a true square wave (one with no zero state).

Final answer

cos(7πα) = 0, so α = 1/14 = 0.071 (a zero interval 25.7° wide).

Third harmonic: 0.332·vd, against 0.424·vd for the square wave (78 %).

Fifth harmonic: 0.110·vd, against 0.255·vd (43 %).

The fundamental falls only to 97.5 % of its square-wave value.

Topic 7 — Single-Phase Inverters

Same fundamental, three ways (the Lab 2 bridge)

Practice, Problem B.1  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsChoosing the control setting for a wanted fundamental, then reading the PWM harmonic table and turning a harmonic voltage into a harmonic current.

The Lab 2 bridge is supplied from vd = 55 V. Its load, between A and B, is L = 5 mH in series with R = 12.5 Ω, and f1 = 60 Hz. It is to produce a fundamental output voltage of 44 V (peak).

The table gives the harmonics of vt for bipolar sinusoidal PWM as the peak value divided by vd. A row marked ± gives the value of each of its two components. With unipolar PWM the rows around mf and 3mf are absent and the rows around 2mf are unchanged.

hmi = 0.20.40.60.81.0

The table gives the harmonics of vt for bipolar sinusoidal PWM at mi = 0.8, as the peak value divided by vd. A row marked ± gives the value of each of its two components. With unipolar PWM the rows around mf and 3mf are absent and the rows around 2mf are unchanged.

Topic 8 — Power Balance and the DC Link

Following the power to the dc side

Practice, Problem C.1  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsThe whole of Topic 8 on one bridge: instantaneous ac power, the dc-side current, the 2ω ripple and the capacitor that absorbs it.

The single-phase inverter shown, an H-bridge operated with sinusoidal PWM, has vd = 400 V and delivers P = 2 kW at unity power factor to its ac terminals at 60 Hz. Its dc side is a source that supplies a constant current id = Id, with the dc-link capacitor C across the bridge input. Take the switches as ideal and neglect switching-frequency components.

(a)Write the instantaneous power at the ac terminals and sketch it over one line period.
(b)Find Id. Sketch the bridge input current id,inv and the capacitor current ic. Ignore their switching-frequency terms: sketch only the average of each over a switching period, not the individual pulses.
(c)Find C for a peak-to-peak ripple of 2 % of vd.
(d)With C = 1 mF, what is the ripple?
(e)The load changes to 2 kW at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. What are Id and the C needed for 2 % ripple now?
(f)Explain, using energy, why the capacitor required is inversely proportional to both vd and Δvd, and why raising the switching frequency does not help.
Final answer
(a)Taking the ac voltage as a cosine at zero phase: p(t) = 2000·[1 + cos 2ω1t] W
(b)Id = 5 A. id,inv = 5 + 5·cos 2ω1t A; the capacitor supplies the pulsating part, ic = 5·cos 2ω1t A.
(c)1.66 mF
(d)13.3 V (3.3 %)
(e)Id = 5 A, unchanged; S = 2.5 kVA, so C = 2.07 mF
(f)The capacitor must buffer a fixed energy S/ω1 every quarter line cycle, set only by the power and the line frequency. It does so by swinging its voltage: ΔE = C·vd·Δvd. The switching frequency does not appear.
Topic 8 — Power Balance and the DC Link

The dc-side current of an inverter and its input filter

Kassakian, Problem 8.15  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsThe dc-link problem as the textbook poses it: with phase-shift control, a real waveform, and an L–C filter instead of a capacitor alone.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book; the operating point is the result of Kassakian's Example 8.1. In part (b), keep only the component of the dc-side current at twice the line frequency and assume all of it flows in Cf.

A full bridge supplied from vd is connected through an inductor L to an ac voltage source vg, as shown. The bridge uses phase-shift control, so vt is the three-level waveform in the figure.

vg = 400·sin(377t) Vvd = 350 VL = 10 mH

The control is set so that 10 kW is delivered to vg with the fundamental of it in phase with vg. That operating point is:

  • the fundamental of it is 50 A (peak), in phase with vg;
  • the fundamental of vt is 442 V (peak) and leads vg by 25.2°;
  • vt is zero for 7.1° on each side of each of its zero crossings, so each zero interval is 14.2° wide.
(a)Calculate and sketch, with values, the current the bridge draws from its dc terminals. You may use the fundamental of it only.
(b)An input filter is added between a dc source Vdc = 350 V and the bridge: a series inductor Lf and a capacitor Cf across the bridge input, as in the second figure. Using reasonable approximations, choose Lf and Cf so that the peak-to-peak ripple current in the dc source is 5 % of the dc current, and the peak-to-peak ripple voltage at the bridge input is 5 % of Vdc.
Final answer
(a)The dc-side current equals +it while vt = +vd, −it while vt = −vd, and zero during the zero states. Using the fundamental of it: a piece of 50·sin θ running from θ = −18.1° (−15.5 A) through the 50 A peak to θ = 147.7° (+26.7 A), then zero for 14.2°, repeating every half cycle. Average = P/vd = 28.6 A.
(b)Estimating the component at twice the line frequency from the fundamental power pulsation gives about 31.6 A (11.05 kVA / 350 V). For 17.5 V peak-to-peak: Cf ≈ 4.8 mF. That ripple voltage across Lf gives 1.43 A peak-to-peak if Lf ≈ 16 mH. This estimate is on the safe side: a Fourier analysis of the actual waveform gives about 26 A, for which Cf ≈ 4.0 mF would do.
Topic 9 — Power Semiconductor Devices

Which quadrants?

Practice, Problem D.1  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsThe Topic 9 method: the on state fixes the sign of the current, the off state fixes the polarity of the voltage, and the device follows.
Quadrants are numbered as in Topic 9, with the switch voltage horizontal and the switch current vertical: I is v > 0, i > 0; II is v < 0, i > 0; III is v < 0, i < 0; IV is v > 0, i < 0. Take the voltage of S1 as positive at its upper terminal and its current as positive downward.

For each of the following, state the sign(s) of the current the switch must conduct when on, the polarity (or polarities) of the voltage it must block when off, the operating quadrants, and a device that realizes it.

(a)S1 of the bridge shown, with the inductor removed so that the load is purely resistive, in square-wave operation.
(b)S1 of the bridge as drawn, with its R–L load.
(c)A switch that connects a 120 V, 60 Hz source to a resistive heater and must be able to turn the heater on or off at any instant in the cycle.
(d)Could the bridge be built using only diodes for its four switches? Explain.
Final answer
(a)Positive current, positive voltage: quadrant I. An IGBT (or MOSFET).
(b)Both current directions, positive voltage: quadrants I and IV. An IGBT with an antiparallel diode, or a MOSFET.
(c)Both current directions and both voltage polarities: all four quadrants. A bidirectional switch.
(d)No. A diode cannot be turned on or off by command and blocks one polarity only. Four diodes with an ac source on the output side form a rectifier, not an inverter.
Topic 9 — Power Semiconductor Devices

A source selector

Practice, Problem D.2  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsThe same method on a circuit you have not seen, where the three switches need three different devices.

Three dc sources are connected through switches Sa, Sb and Sc to a common node X that feeds an inductor and a resistive load. Exactly one switch is on at any time, and the control may select them in any order. Take each switch voltage as positive at its source end and each switch current as positive toward X.

Va = 48 VVb = 24 VVc = 12 V
(a)With iL > 0 at all times, find for each switch the current it conducts when on and the voltage(s) it blocks when off. Choose a device or a combination of devices for each.
(b)Which of the three switches does not need a gate signal? What does it remind you of?
(c)The resistive load is replaced by one that can return energy (a battery, say), so iL may take either sign. Repeat part (a).
Final answer
(a)Sa: positive current, blocks +24 V and +36 V. Quadrant I: an IGBT or MOSFET.

Sb: positive current, blocks −24 V and +12 V. Quadrants I and II: an IGBT in series with a diode. Not a thyristor: Sb must turn off on command when Sc takes over, and it then sees +12 V.

Sc: positive current, blocks −36 V and −12 V. Quadrant II: a diode.

(b)Sc. It conducts whenever the other two are off, like the diode of a buck converter.
(c)Sa: both currents, positive voltage: a MOSFET, or an IGBT with an antiparallel diode. Sb: both currents, both polarities: a bidirectional switch. Sc: both currents, negative voltage: a MOSFET (or IGBT with antiparallel diode) turned over.
Topic 9 — Power Semiconductor Devices

The switches of an inverter feeding an ac source

Kassakian, Problem 8.14  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsWhy every voltage-source bridge has antiparallel diodes: the load current is out of phase with the bridge voltage.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. This combines Kassakian's Problem 8.14 with the last question of his Problem 8.3; the operating point is the result of his Example 8.1.

A full bridge supplied from vd is connected through an inductor L to an ac voltage source vg, as shown. The bridge uses phase-shift control, so vt is the three-level waveform in the figure.

vg = 400·sin(377t) Vvd = 350 VL = 10 mH

The control is set so that 10 kW is delivered to vg with the fundamental of it in phase with vg. That operating point is:

  • the fundamental of it is 50 A (peak), in phase with vg;
  • the fundamental of vt is 442 V (peak) and leads vg by 25.2°;
  • vt is zero for 7.1° on each side of each of its zero crossings, so each zero interval is 14.2° wide.
(a)Find the peak values of the third, fifth and seventh harmonic components of it.
(b)Could switches that conduct current in one direction only be used in this circuit? Explain.
(c)Propose an implementation of the four switches.
Final answer
(a)Each harmonic of vt drives a current through L alone (vg has no harmonics): about 12.2 A at the 3rd, 3.9 A at the 5th and 1.6 A at the 7th, on top of the 50 A fundamental.
(b)No. The fundamental of it lags vt by 25.2°, so at the start of each pulse of vt the current still has the opposite sign: the switches must carry current in both directions.
(c)Each switch blocks +vd only and carries both current directions: a transistor (IGBT or MOSFET) with an antiparallel diode.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

Assumed states in the freewheeling rectifier

Kassakian, Problem 3.2  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsThe method of assumed states, and why a source inductance forces both diodes on together for a while.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Part (c) is added: it is the step from the ideal circuit to the one with Lc.

The half-wave rectifier with freewheeling diode is shown, with vg = Vg·sin ωt. The load is an inductor Ld in series with R, and Ld is large enough that id ≈ Id > 0 at all times. Take the diodes as ideal. For parts (a) and (b), Lc = 0.

(a)Use the method of assumed states to show that D1 and D2 cannot both be on over any interval of ωt.
(b)Show that they cannot both be off either.
(c)Now Lc > 0. Just before ωt = 0, D2 carries Id and ig = 0. Show that just after ωt = 0 neither "D1 on, D2 off" nor "D1 off, D2 on" is consistent. What state must the circuit be in, and what is vd during it?
Final answer
(a)D1 on makes vd = vg; D2 on makes vd = 0. Both hold only if vg = 0, so the state fails at every instant except the zero crossings.
(b)Both off gives id = 0, but Ld holds id = Id > 0.
(c)D1 alone needs ig to jump from 0 to Id, which Lc does not allow. D2 alone gives vD1 = vg > 0, so D1 cannot stay off. Both conduct: vd = 0 and Lc·di_{g}/dt = vg, so ig rises and iD2 = Id − ig falls. This is the commutation interval; it ends when ig reaches Id, at ωt = u.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

Power factor: half-wave against bridge

Kassakian, Problem 3.7/3.12  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsTopic 6's power factor on the two basic diode rectifiers: the same power, very different rms line currents.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Combines Kassakian's Problems 3.7 and 3.12; the numbers in part (c) are added.

Two diode rectifiers each feed a load Ld in series with R, with Ld large enough that id ≈ Id. There is no source inductance (Lc = 0), and vg = Vg·sin ωt.

(a)For the half-wave rectifier with freewheeling diode (first figure), sketch ig over one cycle and find the power factor kp seen by vg.
(b)Repeat for the single-phase diode bridge (second figure).
(c)Each rectifier delivers ⟨vd⟩·Id = 1 kW from a 120 V rms, 60 Hz source. Find Id and the rms line current Ig for each.
(d)In both circuits the fundamental of ig is in phase with vg. What makes the half-wave power factor lower?
Final answer
(a)ig = Id for 0 < ωt < π and 0 for π < ωt < 2π. kp = 2/π = 0.637.
(b)ig = +Id for 0 < ωt < π and −Id for π < ωt < 2π. kp = 2√2/π = 0.900.
(c)Half-wave: Id = 18.5 A, Ig = 13.1 A (S = 1.57 kVA). Bridge: Id = 9.26 A, Ig = 9.26 A (S = 1.11 kVA).
(d)The half-wave ig has a dc component Id/2. From a sinusoidal source it carries no power, but it adds to Ig. Without it the ratio Ig1/Ig would be 0.900, as in the bridge.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

Centre-tapped rectifier with commutation inductance

Kassakian, Problem 3.10  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsCommutation in a circuit not on the slides: find which current changes in Lc, and by how much, before writing u.
Restated in the lecture notation, with numbers added, so you do not need the book.

A centre-tapped transformer secondary is modelled as two equal sources: the upper end is at +vg and the lower end at −vg, both measured from the centre tap, with vg = Vg·sin ωt. Each end feeds a diode through its own inductance Lc (the leakage inductance), as shown: the upper end feeds D1 with current ig1, the lower end feeds D2 with current ig2. The output vd is taken between the joined cathodes and the centre tap. The load is Ld in series with R, with id ≈ Id.

Vg = 170 Vω = 377 rad/sLc = 2 mHId = 20 A
(a)Take Lc = 0. Sketch vd, ig1 and ig2 for 0 < ωt < 2π, and find ⟨vd⟩.
(b)Now Lc = 2 mH. Show that vd = 0 while both diodes conduct, and find the commutation angle u.
(c)Find ⟨vd⟩.
(d)Compare the drop in ⟨vd⟩ with that of a single-phase diode bridge with the same Lc, Vg and Id. Explain the difference.
Final answer
(a)vd = |vg|; ig1 = Id for 0 < ωt < π and ig2 = Id for π < ωt < 2π, each zero otherwise. ⟨vd⟩ = 2Vg/π = 108.2 V.
(b)vd = 0 during the overlap. Xc = 0.754 Ω, cos u = 1 − XcId/Vg, u = 24.3°.
(c)⟨vd⟩ = 2Vg/π − XcId/π = 108.2 − 4.8 = 103.4 V.
(d)The bridge drops 2XcId/π = 9.6 V (⟨vd⟩ = 98.6 V, u = 34.7°), twice as much. In the bridge one Lc carries ig from −Id to +Id, a change of 2Id; here each Lc current changes by Id only.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

A square-wave source and leakage inductance

Kassakian, Problem 3.16  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsThe commutation of Part 1 with straight-line waveforms: the output voltage lost in the rectifier of every isolated converter.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book; the numbers in part (g) are added.

A square-wave voltage vs, +Vs for the first half of each period T and −Vs for the second, drives a diode bridge through a small inductance Lc, as shown. This is the secondary side of an isolated dc–dc converter: vs is the voltage induced in the transformer secondary and Lc is its leakage inductance. The bridge output vd feeds Ld in series with R, with Ld large enough that id ≈ Id. The diodes are ideal.

(a)Take Lc = 0. Sketch and dimension vd and the source current is over one period, in terms of Vs, T and R.
(b)What is ⟨vd⟩ in this case?
(c)Now Lc > 0. Sketch and dimension vd and is in terms of Vs, T, Lc and Id.
(d)Mark on your sketch which diodes conduct in each interval, and the duration tu of each commutation (while is changes).
(e)Find ⟨vd⟩ in terms of Vs, T, Lc and Id.
(f)Sketch ⟨vd⟩ against Id (the load regulation curve).
(g)With Vs = 50 V, T = 10 µs (100 kHz), Lc = 1 µH and Id = 20 A, find tu and ⟨vd⟩.
Final answer
(a)vd = Vs throughout. is = +Id while vs = +Vs and −Id while vs = −Vs, with Id = Vs/R.
(b)⟨vd⟩ = Vs.
(c)After each step of vs, is ramps linearly between +Id and −Id at slope ±Vs/Lc while vd = 0; then vd = Vs for the rest of the half-period.
(d)D1, D4 while is = +Id; D2, D3 while is = −Id; all four during each ramp, which lasts tu = 2LcId/Vs.
(e)⟨vd⟩ = Vs(1 − 2tu/T) = Vs − 4LcId/T, valid while tu ≤ T/2.
(f)A straight line falling from Vs at Id = 0, with slope −4Lc/T, reaching zero at Id = VsT/(4Lc).
(g)tu = 0.8 µs; ⟨vd⟩ = 42 V, 16 % below Vs.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

A commutating resistance instead of an inductance

Kassakian, Problem 3.5  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsWhy the source inductance is called a lossless resistance: replace it with a real one and compare.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book.

In the half-wave rectifier with freewheeling diode shown, Lc is replaced by a resistance Rc. As before vg = Vg·sin ωt, id ≈ Id, and the diodes are ideal. Take RcId ≤ Vg.

(a)Use the method of assumed states to find the state of D1 and D2 over one cycle. Show that both conduct while 0 < vg < RcId.
(b)Show that ⟨vd⟩ = (Vg/π)·[√(1 − y²) − y·cos⁻¹y], where y = RcId/Vg ≤ 1.
(c)Plot ⟨vd⟩/(Vg/π) against y from 0 to 1. On the same axes plot the result with an inductance Lc whose reactance Xc equals Rc: ⟨vd⟩ = (Vg/π)(1 − y/2).
(d)Which of the two drops dissipates power? Where does the energy go in the other case?
Final answer
(a)With θ_{1} = sin⁻¹(RcId/Vg): 0 < ωt < θ_{1}, both on, vd = 0, ig = vg/Rc. θ_{1} < ωt < π − θ_{1}, D1 only, vd = vg − RcId. π − θ_{1} < ωt < π, both on again. π < ωt < 2π, D2 only, vd = 0.
(b)Average vg − RcId over θ_{1} < ωt < π − θ_{1} (divide by 2π), using cos θ_{1} = √(1 − y²) and π/2 − θ_{1} = cos⁻¹y.
(c)With Rc: 1, 0.639, 0.342, 0.119, 0 at y = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, starting with slope −π/2 and reaching zero at Id = Vg/Rc. With Lc: a straight line from 1 to 0.5 over the same range, reaching zero only at y = 2.
(d)Rc turns its drop into heat. Lc stores ½LcId² while ig rises and returns it to vg while ig falls (π to π + u), so its drop dissipates nothing: it only means less power is drawn from vg.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

Half-wave phase control: diode or thyristor freewheeling

Kassakian, Problem 4.4/4.5  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsWhat lets a phase-controlled rectifier invert: a path that keeps vd = vg after vg goes negative.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Combines Kassakian's Problems 4.4 and 4.5.

The half-wave phase-controlled rectifier in the first figure has a thyristor S1 and a freewheeling diode D2, with vg = Vg·sin ωt. The dc side is a large inductor Ld in series with a dc source vo, so id ≈ Id > 0. S1 is fired at ωt = α in every cycle, 0 ≤ α ≤ π. The devices are ideal and there is no source inductance.

(a)Sketch vd over one cycle. Derive ⟨vd⟩ as a function of α and plot it for 0 ≤ α ≤ π.
(b)Can this circuit operate as an inverter, sending power from vo to vg? Explain.
(c)D2 is replaced by a second thyristor S2 (second figure), fired at ωt = π + α. Sketch vd, then derive and plot ⟨vd⟩ against α.
(d)For what range of α can the circuit of part (c) invert, and what must vo be?
Final answer
(a)vd = vg from α to π and 0 elsewhere, while D2 carries Id. ⟨vd⟩ = (Vg/2π)(1 + cos α), from Vg/π at α = 0 to 0 at α = π.
(b)No. D2 clamps vd ≥ 0, so ⟨vd⟩ ≥ 0, and with id > 0 the power ⟨vd⟩Id cannot be negative.
(c)S1 keeps conducting after π until S2 is fired, so vd = vg from α to π + α and 0 from π + α to 2π + α. ⟨vd⟩ = (Vg/π)·cos α, half the thyristor bridge's.
(d)π/2 < α < π, with vo = ⟨vd⟩ = (Vg/π)·cos α < 0: the dc source must reverse its polarity while id stays positive.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

The hybrid bridge

Kassakian, Problem 4.8/4.13  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsTwo thyristors replaced by diodes: a freewheeling path that cuts the reactive power and rules out inversion.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Combines Kassakian's Problems 4.8 and 4.13; part (d) is added.

In the hybrid bridge shown, the upper devices are thyristors S1 and S2 and the lower ones are diodes D3 and D4, with vg = Vg·sin ωt. S1 is fired at ωt = α and S2 at π + α. The dc side is a large inductor Ld in series with a dc source vo, so id ≈ Id > 0. The devices are ideal and there is no source inductance.

(a)Sketch vd and ig for α = 60°, and mark which devices conduct in each interval.
(b)Derive ⟨vd⟩ as a function of α for 0 < α < π, and plot it. Why can this bridge not invert?
(c)Find the power factor kp seen by vg as a function of α.
(d)The hybrid bridge and the four-thyristor bridge are each set for ⟨vd⟩ = Vg/π with the same Id. For each, find α, kp and the reactive power Q drawn from vg.
(e)At α = π/2 the four-thyristor bridge has kp = 0. Reconcile this with what happens on its dc side.
Final answer
(a)α to π: S1, D4 on, vd = vg, ig = Id. π to π + α: S1, D3 on (freewheeling), vd = 0, ig = 0. π + α to 2π: S2, D3 on, vd = −vg, ig = −Id. 2π to 2π + α: S2, D4 on, vd = 0, ig = 0.
(b)⟨vd⟩ = (Vg/π)(1 + cos α), from 2Vg/π to 0. Each leg's thyristor and diode give Id a freewheeling path, so vd ≥ 0 and ⟨vd⟩ cannot go negative.
(c)kp = √2·(1 + cos α)/√(π(π − α)); the fundamental of ig lags vg by α/2.
(d)Hybrid: α = 90°, kp = 0.637, Q = VgI_{d}/π. Four thyristors: α = 60°, kp = 0.450, Q = √3·VgI_{d}/π, 1.73 times as much.
(e)⟨vd⟩ = (2Vg/π)·cos 90° = 0, so the dc side takes P = ⟨vd⟩Id = 0 as well. Energy flows to the dc side while vd > 0 and back while vd < 0, in equal amounts every half-cycle. With ⟨vd⟩ = 0 the source vo is zero, so that energy is stored in Ld: Ld·di_{d}/dt = vd, and id rises and falls a little about Id. This ripple is present at every α (Ld·di_{d}/dt = vd − vo); it is small only because Ld is large, which is what id ≈ Id means. The grid sees the exchange as reactive power, with the fundamental of ig lagging vg by 90°.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

A battery charger with source inductance

Kassakian, Problem 4.12  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsTwo drops in series: the commutation drop 2XcId/π and the battery's own resistance, which here happen to be equal.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book, with the values scaled to a 120 V rms line and a 48 V battery. The inductor L is taken large enough that the charging current is constant.

The battery charger shown is a four-thyristor bridge supplied from vg through an inductance Lc. It charges a battery, modelled as a source EB in series with an internal resistance RB, through an inductor L large enough that the charging current is a constant IB. S1 and S4 are fired at α, and S2 and S3 at π + α.

vg = 170·sin(377t) VLc = 1 mHEB = 48 VRB = 0.240 Ω
(a)Find IB as a function of α, and plot it over the range of α for which the battery charges.
(b)Find α and the commutation angle u for IB = 20 A.
(c)At IB = 20 A, compare the drop in ⟨vd⟩ caused by commutation with the voltage across RB. Which of the two dissipates power?
(d)How would the curve of part (a) change if the battery had no internal resistance?
Final answer
(a)IB = (108.2·cos α − 48)/0.480 A: the commutation drop 2XcIB/π acts like 0.240 Ω, equal to RB. The battery charges for α < 63.7°; for example 125 A at 0°, 95 A at 30°, 59 A at 45° and 13 A at 60°.
(b)α = 57.8°, u = 5.8°.
(c)Both are 4.8 V. RB dissipates 96 W. The commutation drop dissipates nothing: vg supplies ⟨vd⟩IB = 1056 W, which is 96 W less than (2Vg/π)·cos α·IB = 1152 W at the same α.
(d)IB = (108.2·cos α − 48)/0.240 A: the same zero at α = 63.7°, but twice as steep.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

How far can a half-wave converter invert?

Kassakian, Problem 4.7  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsThe inversion limit α + u < π in a circuit whose commutation moves Id, not 2Id.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Kassakian's version also includes the thyristors' turn-off time; here the limit is the lecture's, γ = 0.

The converter shown has a thyristor S1 in series with the source and a second thyristor S2 across the dc side. S1 is fired at α and S2 at π + α. The source has inductance Lc, and the dc side, a large inductor in series with a dc source, carries a constant Id.

vg = 200·sin(2π·400t) VLc = 200 µHId = 40 A
(a)Show that each commutation satisfies cos α − cos(α + u) = XcId/Vg, and explain why the bridge's equation has 2XcId instead.
(b)After S2 has taken over the current, for what angle is S1 reverse-biased? (S2 gets the same angle after S1 takes over.)
(c)Using the extinction-angle limit from the lecture, find the largest α at which the converter can invert, and the largest |⟨vd⟩| it can then deliver.
Final answer
(a)Each commutation moves the current in Lc between 0 and Id, a change of Id; in the bridge ig swings from −Id to +Id. Here Xc = 0.503 Ω and XcId/Vg = 0.101.
(b)γ = π − α − u: from the end of the overlap until vg turns positive at 2π.
(c)The overlap must end before vg turns positive: γ = 0 gives cos α = −1 + XcId/Vg, so α = 154.1° (u = 25.9°) and ⟨vd⟩ = −60.5 V: |⟨vd⟩| ≤ 60.5 V.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

A rectifier that draws current only part of the time

Kassakian, Problem 3.18  ·  Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese & Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2023)
What it drillsPower factor from the waveform alone, and why trimming current near the zero crossings can raise it.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book; part (c) is added.

A rectifier draws a stepped square-wave current from vg = Vg·sin ωt: ig = +Id for β < ωt < π − β, −Id for π + β < ωt < 2π − β, and zero otherwise, as in the figure (0 ≤ β < π/2).

(a)Find the power factor kp at the source as a function of β.
(b)Find the two factors of kp: the ratio Ig1/Ig, and cos φ1, where φ1 is the angle by which the fundamental of ig lags vg.
(c)Evaluate kp for β = 0, 30° and 60°. Which β gives the highest kp? Explain why removing current near the zero crossings can raise it.
Final answer
(a)kp = 2√2·cos β/√(π(π − 2β)).
(b)cos φ1 = 1, since ig is symmetric about the peak of vg, so Ig1/Ig = kp. Ig1 = (2√2/π)·Id·cos β and Ig = Id·√((π − 2β)/π).
(c)0.900, 0.955 and 0.780. The highest is 0.961, at β ≈ 23° (where tan β·(π − 2β) = 1). Near the zero crossings vg is small, so current drawn there adds to Ig but carries almost no power.
Topic 10 — Rectifiers

A boost PFC rectifier

Practice, Problem E.1  ·  ENEL 585 practice problems, Fall 2026
What it drillsPart 3 in numbers: the emulated resistance, the duty ratio that follows the line, and why Vd must stay above the line peak.

The boost PFC rectifier shown draws power from a 120 V rms, 60 Hz line and delivers P = 1 kW to its load at Vd = 400 V. The controller makes the average of iL over each switching period follow |vg|/Re. Take every component as ideal.

(a)Find Re and the peak line current Îg.
(b)Write the duty ratio d(t) in terms of vg and Vd. What are its largest and smallest values over a line cycle?
(c)The same converter is connected to a 230 V rms line instead. Does it still work, and what changes in part (b)? What would happen on that line with Vd = 300 V? The last question needs only a qualitative answer.
Final answer
(a)Re = 14.4 Ω; Îg = 11.8 A.
(b)d(t) = 1 − |vg(t)|/Vd: 1 at the zero crossings, 0.576 at the line peak.
(c)Yes: Vg = 325 V is still below Vd, and the smallest d falls to 0.187 (Re = 52.9 Ω for the same 1 kW). With Vd = 300 V, |vg| exceeds Vd near each line peak: iL then rises even with Q1 off, so the controller loses control of it there.
Topic 11 — Dynamics & Control

The boost converter: model, Gvg and Gvd

Erickson 2e, Problem 7.1/8.21  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Kluwer, 2001)
What it drillsParts 1 and 2 on a converter not on the slides: average, perturb and linearize, the matrix form, then the two standard forms, which component sets each feature, and the RHP zero.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Combines Erickson's Problems 7.1 and 8.21(a, b); the matrix form is added, and Erickson's equivalent-circuit (7.2, 7.3) and impedance (8.21 c, d) parts are left out.

The boost converter shown operates in the continuous conduction mode at D=0.6, with the values on the figure: Q1 is on for a fraction d of each switching period, and d′=1−d. Take every component as ideal and the switching ripple as small. ⟨x⟩Ts is the average of x over one switching period Ts.

(a)Average the inductor voltage and the capacitor current over one switching period to find the averaged model, Ld⟨iL⟩Tsdt and Cd⟨v⟩Tsdt. Which terms make it nonlinear?
(b)Perturb around the operating point, ⟨vg⟩Ts=Vg+v^g, d=D+d^, ⟨iL⟩Ts=IL+i^L and ⟨v⟩Ts=V+v^, and linearize. Find V and IL, and write the small-signal model in the matrix form d𝐱^dt=𝐀𝐱^+𝐁𝐮^,𝐱^=[i^Lv^],𝐮^=[v^gd^] What lets you drop the products of two perturbations?
(c)Find the line-to-output transfer function in the standard form Gvg(s)=Gg011+s/(Qω0)+(s/ω0)2 Give Gg0, f0 and Q in symbols and in numbers.
(d)Find the control-to-output transfer function in the standard form Gvd(s)=Gd01−s/ωz1+s/(Qω0)+(s/ω0)2 Give Gd0 and fz in symbols and in numbers. Is the zero in the left or the right half-plane?
(e)Sketch the magnitude and phase asymptotes of Gvg and of Gvd, labelling the dc gains, f0, the peaks, fz and the slopes.
Final answer
(a)Ld⟨iL⟩Tsdt=⟨vg⟩Ts−d′⟨v⟩Ts and Cd⟨v⟩Tsdt=d′⟨iL⟩Ts−⟨v⟩TsR. The products d′⟨v⟩Ts and d′⟨iL⟩Ts make the model nonlinear.
(b)V=Vg/D′=120 V, IL=V/(D′R)=25 A. The products d^v^ and d^i^L are dropped because the perturbations are much smaller than the dc values (|d^|≪D′). 𝐀=[0−D′/LD′/C−1/(RC)], 𝐁=[1/LV/L0−IL/C].
(c)Gg0=1/D′=2.5 (8.0 dB); ω0=D′/LC, f0=1.11 kHz; Q=D′RC/L=2.76 (8.8 dB).
(d)Gd0=V/D′=300 V (49.5 dBV); ωz=D′2R/L, fz=3.06 kHz. The zero is at s=+ωz: right half-plane.
(e)Gvg: flat at 8.0 dB, 8.8 dB above that at f0, then −40 dB/decade; phase 0 to −180°, asymptote from 730 Hz to 1.68 kHz. Gvd: flat at 49.5 dBV, a peak at f0 (8.8 dB from Q, 9.3 dB with the zero), −40 dB/decade from f0 to fz, −20 dB/decade above; phase 0 to −180° around f0, plus −90° from the RHP zero (asymptote 306 Hz to 30.6 kHz), toward −270°.
Topic 11 — Dynamics & Control

A buck converter with source resistance

Erickson 2e, Problem 7.8/8.17  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Kluwer, 2001)
What it drillsWhat a loss does to the dynamics: one new product in the averaged model, and a resistance that damps the resonant peak.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Combines Erickson's Problems 7.8 and 8.17; the equivalent-circuit part of 7.8 is left out, and the comparison in part (c) is added.

The buck converter shown operates in the continuous conduction mode. Its input source vg has an internal resistance Rg; every other component is ideal, and the switching ripple is small. The capacitor equation is that of the ideal buck, Cd⟨v⟩Tsdt=⟨iL⟩Ts−⟨v⟩TsR.

Vg=120 VD=0.6R=10 Ω
Rg=2 ΩL=550 µHC=100 µF
(a)Find the averaged inductor equation Ld⟨iL⟩Tsdt. Which product in it is not in the ideal buck? Find the operating point V and IL.
(b)Perturb and linearize, by any method, and find the control-to-output transfer function in the standard form Gvd(s)=Gd011+s/(Qω0)+(s/ω0)2 Give Gd0, f0 and Q in symbols and in numbers.
(c)Sketch the magnitude and phase asymptotes of Gvd. Compare Q with its value for Rg=0: what does Rg do to the resonant peak? Why is Gd0 smaller than V/D?
Final answer
(a)Ld⟨iL⟩Tsdt=d(⟨vg⟩Ts−Rg⟨iL⟩Ts)−⟨v⟩Ts; the new product is dRg⟨iL⟩Ts. V=DVgRR+DRg=64.3 V, IL=V/R=6.43 A.
(b)Gvd(s)=(Vg−RgIL)/(LC)s2+s(1RC+DRgL)+kLC with k=1+DRg/R=1.12: Gd0=(Vg−RgIL)/k=95.7 V (39.6 dBV); ω0=k/(LC), f0=718 Hz; Q=kLCL/R+DRgC=1.42 (3.0 dB).
(c)Flat at 39.6 dBV, 3.0 dB above that at f0, then −40 dB/decade; phase 0 to −180°, asymptote 319 Hz to 1.62 kHz. With Rg=0, Q=RC/L=4.26 (12.6 dB): Rg damps the resonance, cutting the peak from 12.6 dB to 3.0 dB. Gd0 is below V/D=107 V because a larger d also raises IL and so the drop across Rg.
Topic 11 — Dynamics & Control

A PWM with a triangle wave

Erickson 2e, Problem 7.14  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Kluwer, 2001)
What it drillsThe PWM gain 1/VM for a triangle wave in place of the slides' sawtooth.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Part (c) is added.

In the pulse-width modulator shown, a comparator turns Q1 on while the control voltage vc is above the triangle wave vtri of panel (b), and off while it is below. Take vc constant over each switching period.

(a)What is the switching frequency fs?
(b)Find the duty ratio d as a function of vc. Over what range of vc does it hold?
(c)For small changes, d=D+d^ and vc=VC+v^c. Find the PWM gain d^/v^c: what is VM for this triangle wave? What VC gives D=0.6?
Final answer
(a)fs=1/(50 μs)=20 kHz.
(b)vtri is below vc for a fraction (vc+2 V)/(4 V) of each period: d=0.5+vc4 V, for −2 V≤vc≤2 V (d=0 below that range, 1 above it).
(c)d^/v^c=1/(4 V)=0.25 V−1, so VM=4 V, the peak-to-peak height of the triangle wave. D=0.6 needs VC=0.4 V.
Topic 11 — Dynamics & Control

The loop gain of a boost regulator

Erickson 2e, Problem 9.3  ·  Erickson & Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 2nd ed. (Kluwer, 2001)
What it drillsPart 3 end to end: build T from the blocks, read fc and the phase margin, see what the loop does at dc, then how the output follows the reference: 1/H where |T| ≫ 1, T/H where |T| ≪ 1.
Restated in the lecture notation, so you do not need the book. Erickson's parts (a) and (b) are parts (b) and (c) here; his (c) and (d), the closed loop seen from the line, come later in the course and are left out. Parts (a), (d) and (e) are added; (e) is the reference-to-output part of Erickson's 9.4.

The boost converter of Erickson 7.1/8.21, the first Topic 11 problem (D=0.6, values on the figure) is regulated by the loop shown. Every element is ideal. The sensor gain is H=1/24 and the reference vref=5 V; the PWM has VM=4 V, and the compensator is Gc(s)=250/s, with s in rad/s. The boost's Gd0 is positive, so the loop needs no −1 block and the loop gain is T=HGcGvdVM

(a)What output voltage V makes Hv=vref?
(b)The converter's control-to-output transfer function (from Erickson 7.1/8.21) is Gvd(s)=Gd01−s/ωz1+s/(Qω0)+(s/ω0)2 with Gd0=300 V, f0=1.11 kHz, Q=2.76 and fz=3.06 kHz. Write T(s) as a product of factors, and sketch its magnitude and phase asymptotes, labelling every corner frequency, Q and slope.
(c)Find the crossover frequency fc and the phase margin ϕm. Is the loop stable?
(d)The error is v^e=v^ref/(1+T). What is |T| at dc, and so what steady-state error does the loop leave for a constant vref?
(e)The output follows the reference as v^v^ref=1HT1+T Sketch its magnitude asymptotes from the two approximations, v^/v^ref≈1/H where |T|≫1 and v^/v^ref≈T/H where |T|≪1, and label the low-frequency gain and the slopes. At fc, |T|=1 and |1+T|=2sin(ϕm/2): find |v^/v^ref| there. Is |T|≪1 at every frequency above fc? Where is your sketch least accurate?
Final answer
(a)Hv=vref gives V=vref/H=120 V.
(b)T(s)=ωTs·1−s/ωz1+s/(Qω0)+(s/ω0)2, with ωT=250HGd0/VM=781 rad/s, f0=1.11 kHz, Q=2.76, fz=3.06 kHz. Magnitude: −20 dB/decade; at f0 a peak above that asymptote (8.8 dB from Q, 9.3 dB with the zero); −60 dB/decade from f0 to fz; −40 dB/decade above fz. Phase: −90° at low frequency; the quadratic adds −180° (asymptote 730 Hz to 1.68 kHz) and the RHP zero −90° (asymptote 306 Hz to 30.6 kHz), toward −360°.
(c)fc≈ωT/2π=124 Hz from the asymptote (exact: 126 Hz). ∠T(fc)=−90°−2.4° (quadratic)−2.3° (RHP zero)=−94.7°, so ϕm=85°. From the straight-line phase asymptotes instead, ϕm=90°: fc is below where both phase asymptotes start (306 Hz for the RHP zero, 730 Hz for the quadratic), so neither has fallen yet. T has no RHP poles and |T| crosses 1 once: stable.
(d)Gc=250/s grows without bound as s→0, so |T|→∞ at dc and v^e=v^ref/(1+T)→0: a constant vref leaves no steady-state error, and V=vref/H exactly.
(e)1/H=24 (27.6 dB) up to the asymptotes' crossover, fc≈124 Hz; then |T|/H: −20 dB/decade to f0 (2.7, 8.6 dB), with the resonant peak of T there, −60 dB/decade to fz, −40 dB/decade above. At fc, |1+T|=2sin42.6°=1.35, so |v^/v^ref|=24/1.35=17.7 (25.0 dB): below 1/H, no peak at fc with an 85° margin. No: the resonance lifts |T| back to 0.33 at f0, which is not ≪1, so the sketch is least accurate near f0. There the exact curve sits well above the T/H asymptote: 22 dB near 1.04 kHz.
